chapters.title: The Week of the Bake-Off
chapters.text:
The ovens at the Rolling Pin Bakery were warm long before the sun climbed over Pennywhistle Harbor. Hattie Bramble tied back her silver hair, switched on the radio, and began rolling out cinnamon dough while the gulls complained outside. Biscuit, her orange tabby, supervised from the windowsill with the serious air of a cat who expected a reward for his trouble.

By seven o'clock the little bell over the door had not stopped ringing, and everyone seemed to carry the same news. Lionel Crane, the famous television critic, was coming to judge the Harvest Bake-Off. Abe Tolliver, still smelling of salt and bait, bought two blueberry muffins and announced that Crane had once made a grown chef cry on national television. "Gave a pie one star because the crust was shy," Abe said darkly.

Hattie laughed and wrapped his muffins in waxed paper, but she felt a small flutter of nerves all the same. Across the square, the windows of the Sugar and Spoon bakery glowed gold. Her friend Delia Fairweather was surely up early too, fussing over the plum cake she planned to enter.

When the morning rush finally eased, Hattie took out her little green notebook and wrote the date at the top of a fresh page. She had kept notes on recipes, customers, and village doings for years, and something told her this week would need plenty of pages. Biscuit yawned, thoroughly unimpressed, and went back to sleep in the sun.

chapters.title: A Very Particular Guest
chapters.text:
Lionel Crane arrived at the Gull's Rest Inn the next afternoon in a long silver car that looked far too grand for the gravel drive. Hattie happened to be standing in the front hall with a basket of welcome scones, because Rupert Ashby, the innkeeper, had ordered two dozen to make a good impression.

The critic was tall and thin, with a silk scarf and eyebrows that seemed permanently raised. He lifted a scone, sniffed it, and set it down again. "Dry," he declared. "Dry as a Sunday sermon, and far too much orange zest." Hattie's cheeks went warm, but she only smiled. Thirty years of teaching seventh grade had given her a very thick skin.

Behind Lionel came a small, quiet woman carrying three suitcases and a padded case. This was Colette Marsh, who had been his assistant for twelve years. While Rupert fussed over the luggage, Colette knelt and opened the padded case with great care. Nested in tissue paper lay a fine white teacup painted with a gold monogram. "Mr. Crane drinks only from his own," Colette explained softly. "And never with honey. He can't abide it." "Quite right," Lionel sniffed. "Hotel china is a crime."

On the walk home, Hattie took out her green notebook and wrote down the teacup, the scarf, and the insult to her scones, in that order. Then, for good measure, she underlined the insult twice.

chapters.title: Dinner with Daggers Drawn
chapters.text:
The welcome dinner was held in the long dining room of the Gull's Rest Inn, under a chandelier that tinkled whenever the wind gusted off the bay. Hattie sat beside Winnie Calloway, with a fine view of everyone at the table. Lionel Crane held court at the head of it. He sent back the chowder for being lukewarm, then praised the bread so faintly that it sounded like an insult.

When Delia Fairweather passed him the butter, he peered at her. "Boston, wasn't it? That sad little cafe with the soggy tarts?" Delia's fork clattered onto her plate. Hattie remembered, with a pang, that one cruel review from Lionel had closed Delia's first cafe years ago.

Rupert Ashby fared no better. Lionel remarked on the peeling paint and the creaky stairs, and Rupert's knuckles went white around his wineglass. Gordon Pike, the harbor master and chairman of the bake-off committee, laughed too loudly at every joke until Lionel murmured, "We must talk about the old scores, Gordon." After that, Gordon stopped laughing altogether. At the far end sat Imogen Vale, Lionel's niece, with paint on her cuffs. She never once called him uncle, and she left before dessert.

Only Colette Marsh seemed calm, quietly refilling Lionel's water glass. "Well," Winnie whispered over her pudding, "if looks could do harm, that man would need a bodyguard." Hattie said nothing, but beneath the tablecloth she was already writing in her notebook.

chapters.title: Steam in the Blue Suite
chapters.text:
On the morning of the bake-off, Hattie was up even earlier than usual. Rupert had ordered a tray of almond croissants for his guests, and the sky over the harbor was still pale pink when she carried the box through the kitchen door of the Gull's Rest Inn. Dottie Quill, the housekeeper, was already at the stove. "Bless you, Hattie," she said. "Mr. Crane wants his breakfast brought up to the Blue Suite, and if I climb those stairs once more my knees will file a complaint."

So Hattie climbed them herself, balancing the tray. The door of the Blue Suite stood open a few inches. Through the gap she glimpsed a little travel kettle on the dresser, steam curling from its spout, and beside it the monogrammed cup she had seen unpacked. The air smelled of tea, but with a sharp, green edge to it, like a meadow after rain.

"Leave it on the table outside," called a voice from deeper in the room. Hattie could not quite tell whose it was. She set down the tray and tiptoed away, feeling oddly like a schoolgirl caught passing notes. Downstairs, Dottie poured her a cup of coffee and chattered about the judging.

On the walk back to the Rolling Pin, Hattie paused by a lamppost and wrote in her green notebook: kettle, steam, green smell. She could not have said why. It simply seemed worth remembering.

chapters.title: Trouble in the Tea Tent
chapters.text:
By ten o'clock the striped tea tent on the village green was packed to its canvas walls. Long tables groaned under pies, tarts, loaves, and layer cakes, each with a numbered card. Hattie had entered her maple pecan pie, mostly to keep Winnie company, though Winnie had entered nothing and appointed herself chief taster of crumbs.

Gordon Pike rang a little brass bell, and the judging began. Lionel Crane moved down the table with Colette at his elbow, holding his notes. He looked pale, Hattie thought, and he squinted at the bunting as though the light bothered him. "Too sweet," he said of a lemon bar. "Tragic," he said of a rhubarb crumble. He tasted Hattie's pie and pronounced it "adequate," which from Lionel was practically a hug.

Then he reached Delia's plum cake, and the whole tent seemed to hold its breath. Lionel took one forkful and chewed slowly. He opened his mouth to speak, but no words came. His hand fluttered to his chest, the fork slipped from his fingers, and he sank sideways against the table, scattering programs onto the grass.

Rupert Ashby shouted for a doctor. Within minutes an ambulance bumped across the green, lights flashing, and Lionel was carried away on a stretcher. In the hush that followed, Hattie stood very still, her heart thumping. Beside the overturned chair lay the half-eaten slice of plum cake, glistening and dark.

chapters.title: Grim News on the Green
chapters.text:
The tea tent emptied slowly, like a teapot draining. Hattie stayed behind to gather the scattered programs, and Biscuit, who had followed her from the bakery, sat beneath a table with his tail wrapped tight around his paws.

Late in the afternoon, Deputy Sam Bramble came striding across the green. Hattie had watched her nephew grow from a freckled boy who stole cookie dough into a tall young man with a badge, but she had never seen him look so solemn. "Aunt Hattie," he said quietly, taking off his hat. "Mr. Crane died at the county hospital an hour ago. The doctor thinks it might have been poison." Hattie sat down hard on a folding chair. "Poison? At the bake-off?"

"I shouldn't tell you anything," Sam said, which meant he was about to tell her more. "The county is sending a detective. Until she gets here, nobody touches the food." The detective arrived soon after, a brisk woman in a gray raincoat who introduced herself as Lorna Hask. She glanced over the tables, asked three sharp questions, and pointed straight at the plum cake. "That one," she said. "Bag it."

Across the tent, Delia Fairweather pressed a hand to her mouth as Sam lifted the cake into an evidence box. Hattie scooped up Biscuit and held him close. She did not believe for a moment that Delia had harmed anyone. But she could see exactly how it looked.

chapters.title: Something in the Garden
chapters.text:
The next morning was gray and still, and the whole village seemed to be holding its breath. Hattie closed the bakery for an hour and took Biscuit for his walk. Biscuit did not believe in leashes, but he trotted at her heels like a small orange dog, stopping now and then to glare at a sparrow.

Their path led past the Gull's Rest Inn and its old walled garden. The brick walls were thick with ivy, and the wooden gate hung slightly open. Biscuit slipped through before Hattie could stop him. "Come back here, you rascal," she whispered, and followed. The garden was lovely even in October, full of asters, late roses, and seed heads rattling in the breeze.

Along the far wall stood a row of tall foxglove, a few purple bells still clinging to the stems. But several stalks had been cut off near the ground. The ends were clean and pale, the sap still damp to the touch. Hattie frowned. Her grandmother had grown foxglove and warned her never to let the leaves near the kitchen. The plant was beautiful, but it could stop a heart.

She glanced up at the windows of the inn, half expecting a face to appear. None did. Biscuit sniffed the cut stalks, sneezed, and looked up at her as if to ask what she meant to do about it. "I'm going to write it down," Hattie told him, reaching for her green notebook. "That's what I'm going to do."

chapters.title: Whispers About Delia
chapters.text:
By lunchtime the whole of Pennywhistle Harbor seemed to have decided what had happened, and none of it was kind. Hattie heard it in the bakery line, between orders of rye bread and pumpkin muffins. "Everyone knows she hated him," said a woman from the church choir, lowering her voice so that only half the shop could hear. "He ruined her in Boston." "And it was her cake he ate," added the postman, accepting his change with a meaningful look.

Hattie set down the tongs harder than she meant to. "Delia Fairweather has fed half this village through two blizzards and a power outage," she said. "I won't hear another word."

The bell jingled, and Winnie Calloway hurried in from the bookshop next door, her scarf askew and her eyes bright with news. "Detective Hask questioned Delia for two whole hours," she whispered across the counter. "And the Sugar and Spoon has a sign saying closed until further notice. Poor lamb." Hattie looked out across the square. Delia's shop stood dark and silent, its pretty blue awning sagging in the damp. She pictured her friend alone inside among the mixing bowls, listening to the town turn against her.

Biscuit wound around her ankles and gave a firm meow, as if he had reached the same conclusion. "You're right," Hattie said, brushing the flour from her hands. "Winnie, mind the counter for ten minutes. I'm taking Delia a pie, and then I'm going to find out what really happened."

chapters.title: The Empty Hook
chapters.text:
That afternoon Hattie returned to the Gull's Rest Inn with a tin of ginger cookies for Dottie Quill, who had looked so frazzled at the bake-off. She found the housekeeper in the back garden, pinning sheets to the line. "You're an angel," Dottie said, taking a cookie. "Mr. Ashby wants twine from the potting shed, but my hands are full. Would you mind?"

The potting shed stood in a corner of the walled garden, a crooked little building with a mossy roof. Inside it smelled of damp soil and old clay pots. A pegboard covered one whole wall, and someone very tidy had painted the outline of each tool in white: rake, hoe, spade, hand fork, and a long pruning saw. Every tool hung neatly inside its outline but one. Halfway up the board, a sturdy brass hook stood empty, and the painted shape around it was unmistakable. It was the outline of a pair of garden shears.

Hattie found the twine and carried it back out. "Dottie," she asked lightly, "has anyone borrowed the garden shears lately?" Dottie frowned. "Not that I know of. Mr. Ashby is fussy about that pegboard. He'd have a fit if anything went missing."

"I expect they'll turn up," Hattie said. But walking home, she thought of the cut foxglove stalks, so clean and straight. She opened her green notebook, wrote one word, and underlined it twice.

chapters.title: Cocoa and a Suspect List
chapters.text:
After closing time, Hattie locked the Rolling Pin and slipped next door to Winnie's bookshop. The shop was dim and cozy, lit only by a green lamp on the counter. Winnie had two mugs of cocoa waiting, each crowned with a lopsided marshmallow, and Biscuit had already claimed the armchair by the radiator. "Right," said Winnie. "Who would want that dreadful man gone?"

Hattie opened her green notebook to a clean page. "We go by what we saw," she said in her old classroom voice. "No guessing." "Rupert Ashby, then," said Winnie. "Lionel insulted his inn to his face." Hattie wrote it down. "Gordon Pike. Lionel wanted to talk about the old scores, and Gordon went white as flour." "Imogen Vale," Winnie added, licking cocoa from her lip. "His own niece, and she wouldn't even say goodnight. Family quarrels run deepest."

"And Colette Marsh," Hattie said slowly. "She knew his habits better than anyone. His teacup, his schedule, everything." Winnie tapped the page. "You have to put Delia down too, you know. Fair's fair."

Hattie sighed and wrote the name, though her pen pressed hard enough to dent the paper beneath. Five names now sat in a neat column, and below them, the shears and the foxglove. Outside, the harbor bell clanged softly. Biscuit stretched, yawned, and curled into a tighter ball, as if to say the case would keep until morning.
